records.title: Global deformation datum
records.label: def:global_datum
records.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Global deformation datum]\label{def:global_datum}
A global deformation datum consists of the following objects.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A residual representation \(\bar\rho\).
\item For every \(v\in S\), a framed local deformation ring \(R_v^\square\).
\item A quotient \(R_v^{\tau_v}\) representing the chosen local condition whenever such a quotient is known to exist.
\item A global deformation ring \(R^\square\) with a continuous local map
\[
R^{\mathrm{loc}}:=\wideotimes_{v\in S,\OO}R_v^\square
\longrightarrow R^\square.
\]
\item The induced global ring with local conditions
\[
R^{\tau}:=R^\square\wideotimes_{R^{\mathrm{loc}}}R^{\mathrm{loc},\tau},
\qquad
R^{\mathrm{loc},\tau}:=\wideotimes_{v\in S,\OO}R_v^{\tau_v}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

records.title: Completed tensor quotient
records.label: thm:tensor_quotient
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Completed tensor quotient]\label{thm:tensor_quotient}
Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\) be complete Noetherian local \(\OO\) algebras with common residue field \(k\). Let \(I_i\subseteq R_i\) be closed ideals. Put
\[
R^{\mathrm{loc}}=R_1\wideotimes_{\OO}\cdots\wideotimes_{\OO}R_s
\]
and let \(J\) be the closed ideal generated by the images of the \(I_i\). Then there is a canonical isomorphism
\[
\boxed{
(R_1/I_1)\wideotimes_{\OO}\cdots\wideotimes_{\OO}(R_s/I_s)
\cong
R^{\mathrm{loc}}/J.
}
\]
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex: Both rings represent the same functor on complete local \(\OO\) algebras with residue field \(k\). A continuous map from either ring to such an algebra \(A\) is the same as a collection of continuous maps \(R_i\to A\) whose restrictions to \(\OO\) agree and which kill every \(I_i\). The universal property of the completed tensor product gives a unique map from \(R^{\mathrm{loc}}\), and killing all \(I_i\) is equivalent to killing \(J\). The two representing objects are therefore canonically isomorphic.

records.title: Finite adequacy certificate
records.label: thm:s3_adequacy
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Finite adequacy certificate]\label{thm:s3_adequacy}
The standard representation of \(S_3\) over \(\FF_7\) is adequate. More precisely,
\[
H^0(S_3,\ad^0V)=0,
\qquad
H^1(S_3,\FF_7)=0,
\qquad
H^1(S_3,\ad^0V)=0,
\]
and
\[
\ad^0V\cong\operatorname{sgn}\oplus V.
\]
The sign summand is detected by an eigenprojector of a three cycle, and the standard summand is detected by an eigenprojector of a transposition.
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
The commutant of the standard representation consists of scalars. The only trace zero scalar is zero, so \(H^0(S_3,\ad^0V)=0\). Since \(6\) is invertible in \(\FF_7\), averaging contracts positive degree group cochains. Thus \(H^1(S_3,M)=0\) for every \(\FF_7[S_3]\) module \(M\).

The character of \(\ad^0V\) has values \((3,-1,0)\) on the identity, transposition, and three cycle classes. It is the sum of the sign character and the standard character, which gives the displayed decomposition.

Write a trace zero matrix as
\[
W(a,b,c)=
\begin{pmatrix}
a&b\\
c&-a
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The matrix
\[
W_{\mathrm{sgn}}=W(2,3,4)
\]
spans the sign summand. The projector onto the eigenvalue \(2\) of \(t\) is
\[
P_{t,2}=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&4\\
3&6
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\[
\Tr(P_{t,2}W_{\mathrm{sgn}})=3\neq0.
\]
The matrix
\[
W_{\mathrm{std}}=W(6,4,3)
\]
belongs to the standard summand. The projector onto the eigenvalue \(1\) of \(s\) is
\[
P_{s,1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&4\\
0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\[
\Tr(P_{s,1}W_{\mathrm{std}})=6\neq0.
\]
Every irreducible summand of \(\ad^0V\) is therefore detected.
records.proof_route: Construct the S3 action over ZMod 7, identify it with the standard representation, prove absolute irreducibility, trace-zero adjoint invariants and an actual sign-plus-standard decomposition. Prove H1 vanishing by a finite-group averaging/cochain argument. Check the two explicit eigenprojectors and nonzero trace pairings.
records.acceptance: All printed cohomology, decomposition, and detection clauses plus agreement with a precisely specified adequacy definition.
records.formalization_questions: Matrix identities alone are partial coverage. Character values alone are not a Lean representation equivalence. The exact adequacy convention and the imported definition need a later primary-source check.
records.coverage_note: The actual S3 permutation action on the sum-zero subspace of F7^3 is linked to the displayed two-dimensional matrices by a representation equivalence. Faithfulness, coefficient change, absolute irreducibility and splitting of every characteristic polynomial are checked. The actual trace-zero conjugation representation has zero invariants and is equivariantly isomorphic to sign plus standard. Finite-group averaging proves vanishing of actual Mathlib H1 for both the trivial and adjoint representations; the actual H0 comparison gives the stated zero-th cohomology. Canonical eigenprojectors detect every irreducible adjoint submodule, with the literal sign and standard witnesses and trace values 3 and 6 checked. The four adequacy clauses and ambient conditions are assembled without an external adequacy theorem assumption. The original statement is unchanged; its expanded proof is recorded separately.
records.review_verdict: proved as written in the declared context
records.revised_proof_tex:
The coordinate map
\[
(a,b)\longmapsto(a,-a+b,-b)
\]
identifies the displayed matrices with the permutation action on the sum zero subspace of \(\FF_7^3\). This action is faithful. The four matrices \(1,s,t,st\) span \(M_2\) over every field of characteristic seven: the determinant of their coordinate matrix is \(4\ne0\). A subspace stable under the group is therefore stable under every endomorphism, so the representation is absolutely irreducible. The characteristic polynomials of the identity, transpositions, and three cycles are respectively
\[
(X-1)^2,\qquad (X-1)(X+1),\qquad (X-2)(X-4).
\]
Thus all eigenvalues already lie in \(\FF_7\).

A trace zero matrix fixed by conjugation by both \(s\) and \(t\) is zero, as follows by comparing its four entries. This proves \(H^0(S_3,\ad^0V)=0\). For any \(\FF_7[S_3]\) module \(M\) and one cocycle \(f\), put
\[
u=-6^{-1}\sum_{h\in S_3}f(h).
\]
Summing \(f(gh)=g f(h)+f(g)\) over \(h\) gives \(gu-u=f(g)\). Hence every one cocycle is a coboundary and \(H^1(S_3,M)=0\), giving both asserted first cohomology vanishings.

Write
\[
W(a,b,c)=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Z=W(2,3,4),\quad A=W(1,1,2),\quad B=W(1,5,6).
\]
The three coordinate columns have determinant \(3\ne0\). Under conjugation,
\[
sZ=-Z,\quad tZ=Z,\qquad
sA=-A,\quad sB=A+B,\quad tA=B,\quad tB=-A-B.
\]
Consequently \((z,(a,b))\mapsto zZ+aA+bB\) is an equivariant isomorphism from \(\operatorname{sgn}\oplus V\) to \(\ad^0V\).

The sign witness is \(W_{\mathrm{sgn}}=Z\), while
\(W_{\mathrm{std}}=W(6,4,3)=3A+3B\) belongs to the standard summand. The corresponding projectors and trace pairings are
\[
P_{t,2}=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\3&6\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \Tr(P_{t,2}W_{\mathrm{sgn}})=3\ne0,
\]
\[
P_{s,1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \Tr(P_{s,1}W_{\mathrm{std}})=6\ne0.
\]
For an operator \(D\) with \((D-\alpha I)(D-\beta I)=0\) and \(\alpha\ne\beta\), the canonical projector is
\[
P_{D,\alpha}=(\alpha-\beta)^{-1}(D-\beta I).
\]
Its image equals \(\ker((D-\alpha I)^n)\) for every \(n\ge1\), and it kills \(\ker((D-\beta I)^n)\). This identifies the displayed matrices with the generalized eigenspace projectors required in the adequacy definition.

For detection on every irreducible submodule, one can check the stronger assertion that canonical projectors detect every nonzero matrix. In addition to the two projectors above, use
\[
P_{s,-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
P_{tst^{-1},1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\4&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The four trace pairings with these matrices have trivial common kernel in \(M_2(\FF_7)\), by row reduction. Every irreducible adjoint submodule contains a nonzero matrix, so some canonical projector has nonzero trace pairing on that submodule. This verifies the last adequacy clause and completes the certificate.

records.title: Functorial group algebra transfer
records.label: prop:group_algebra_transfer
records.statement_tex:
\begin{proposition}[Functorial group algebra transfer]\label{prop:group_algebra_transfer}
A group homomorphism \(q:\Delta'\to\Delta\) induces an \(\OO\) algebra homomorphism
\[
q_*:\OO[\Delta']\longrightarrow\OO[\Delta].
\]
If \(q\) is surjective, then \(q_*\) is surjective. Augmentation commutes with the transfer:
\[
\epsilon_\Delta q_*=\epsilon_{\Delta'}.
\]
\end{proposition}
records.proof_tex: Extend \(q\) linearly from the group basis. Multiplicativity follows from \(q(gh)=q(g)q(h)\). Surjectivity follows because every basis element of \(\OO[\Delta]\) has a preimage. Both augmentation maps send every group element to one, which gives the final identity.
records.proof_route: Extend a group homomorphism on basis elements of the group algebra. Prove multiplicativity, augmentation compatibility, and surjectivity by lifting finite basis support.
records.acceptance: An actual algebra homomorphism with the stated identities and a proof of surjectivity when the group map is surjective.
records.coverage_note: Actual algebra homomorphism on the group basis, surjectivity from the supplied group surjection, augmentation compatibility, and identity/composition laws. Valid for arbitrary monoids.

records.title: Residual augmentation algebra
records.label: thm:residual_augmentation_algebra
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Residual augmentation algebra]\label{thm:residual_augmentation_algebra}
Suppose
\[
\Delta\cong
\prod_{i=1}^{r}C_{p^{n_i}}.
\]
Choose generators \(\gamma_i\), and let \(X_i=\gamma_i-1\). Then
\[
\boxed{
k[\Delta]
\cong
k[X_1,\ldots,X_r]
\big/
(X_1^{p^{n_1}},\ldots,X_r^{p^{n_r}}).
}
\]
The augmentation ideal is generated by the \(X_i\), and \(k[\Delta]\) is local.
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
In characteristic \(p\),
\[
(1+X_i)^{p^{n_i}}-1=X_i^{p^{n_i}}.
\]
Thus the assignment \(X_i\mapsto\gamma_i-1\) gives a surjective homomorphism from the displayed truncated polynomial ring to \(k[\Delta]\). Both sides have dimension \(\prod_ip^{n_i}=\abs{\Delta}\) over \(k\), so the map is an isomorphism. The quotient by the ideal generated by the \(X_i\) is \(k\). Since each \(X_i\) is nilpotent, that ideal is the unique maximal ideal.
records.proof_route: For a supplied product decomposition of the finite abelian p-group, send each polynomial variable to its generator minus one. Prove the p-power relations, construct the quotient map, and prove it bijective using explicit bounded monomial bases or inverse maps. Identify the augmentation ideal and unique maximal ideal.

Supplied group decompositions are transported explicitly. Empty products and trivial cyclic factors are included.

records.revised_proof_tex:
The first assertion follows from locality in \cref{thm:residual_augmentation_algebra}. For the general finite \(p\) group assertion, let \(e\in k[G]\) be idempotent and write \(\epsilon:k[G]\to k\) for augmentation. Suppose \(\epsilon(e)=0\) and \(e\ne0\). The \(\FF_p\) span \(W\) of the left translates \(ge\) is a nonzero finite dimensional \(\FF_p\) vector space, stable under \(G\). Its cardinality is divisible by \(p\). The orbit counting formula implies that its fixed point set also has cardinality divisible by \(p\). Since zero is fixed, there is a nonzero fixed vector \(v\in W\).

A vector in the regular representation fixed by all left translations has constant coefficients. Consequently \(ve=\epsilon(e)v=0\). On the other hand, \(e^2=e\) implies \(we=w\) for every \(w\in W\), hence \(ve=v\), a contradiction. Thus every idempotent of augmentation zero is zero. Since \(\epsilon(e)^2=\epsilon(e)\) in the field \(k\), either \(\epsilon(e)=0\) or \(\epsilon(e)=1\); in the latter case apply the preceding argument to \(1-e\).

records.statement_tex:
\begin{standardfact}[Iwasawa limit]\label{fact:iwasawa_limit}
For \(\Delta_m=(\ZZ/p^m\ZZ)^r\), the inverse limit of \(\OO[\Delta_m]\) is the Iwasawa algebra
\[
\OO[[\ZZ_p^r]]\cong\OO[[X_1,\ldots,X_r]],
\]
where \(X_i\) corresponds to a chosen topological generator minus one \cite{RibesZalesskii2010}.
\end{standardfact}

records.title: Support and near faithfulness
records.label: def:support_near_faithful
records.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Support and near faithfulness]\label{def:support_near_faithful}
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(M\) be an \(R\) module. Its support is
\[
\Supp_R(M)
=
\{\frakp\in\Spec R:M_{\frakp}\neq0\}.
\]
If \(R\) is Noetherian and \(M\) is finite, then \(M\) is \emph{nearly faithful} when \(\Ann_R(M)\) is a nilpotent ideal.
\end{definition}

records.title: Finite module support
records.label: thm:finite_module_support
records.proof_tex:
Let \(\frakp\in\Spec R\). If \(\Ann_R(M)\not\subseteq\frakp\), choose
\(a\in\Ann_R(M)\setminus\frakp\). The element \(a\) becomes a unit in
\(R_{\frakp}\), so \(M_{\frakp}=0\).

Conversely, suppose \(M_{\frakp}=0\). Choose generators
\(m_1,\ldots,m_d\) of \(M\). For each \(i\), there is an element
\(s_i\notin\frakp\) such that \(s_im_i=0\). The product
\(s=s_1\cdots s_d\) lies outside \(\frakp\) and annihilates every generator.
Thus \(s\in\Ann_R(M)\setminus\frakp\). This proves the equality.

records.title: Fitting support criterion
records.label: thm:fitting_support
records.proof_tex:
If \(M=0\), the statement follows from the usual convention \(\Fitt_0(0)=R\). Assume \(M\neq0\), and choose a finite presentation
\[
R^m\xrightarrow{A}R^n\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0
\]
with \(n\geq1\).
The zeroth Fitting ideal is generated by the \(n\) by \(n\) minors of \(A\). After localization at a prime \(\frakp\), the module \(M_{\frakp}\) vanishes exactly when \(A_{\frakp}\) is surjective. A map onto the free module \(R_{\frakp}^n\) is surjective exactly when one maximal minor is a unit. Thus \(M_{\frakp}=0\) exactly when \(\Fitt_0^R(M)\not\subseteq\frakp\).

records.title: Near faithfulness is full support
records.label: thm:near_faithful_full_support
records.proof_tex:
By \cref{thm:finite_module_support}, full support is equivalent to
\[
V\bigl(\Ann_R(M)\bigr)=\Spec R.
\]
This holds exactly when \(\Ann_R(M)\) is contained in every prime ideal, hence in the nilradical. Because \(R\) is Noetherian, the ideal \(\Ann_R(M)\) is finitely generated. An ideal generated by finitely many nilpotent elements is nilpotent. This proves the equivalence of the first three conditions. If \(R\) is reduced, its nilradical is zero.
records.proof_route: Use support=V(Ann), the intersection-of-primes description of the nilradical, and finite generation of the annihilator in a Noetherian ring to turn nil generators into a nilpotent ideal.

records.formalization_questions: Nilpotent ideal means there is one common power equal to bottom, not only pointwise nilpotence without a finite-generation argument.
records.coverage_note: All three conditions and reduced-ring faithfulness. Near faithfulness is ideal nilpotence. Some constituent implications require fewer hypotheses than the manuscript.

records.title: Support after a quotient
records.label: thm:quotient_support
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Support after a quotient]\label{thm:quotient_support}
Let \(R\) be Noetherian, let \(I\subseteq R\) be an ideal, and let \(M\) be a finite \(R\) module. Under the canonical identification
\[
\Spec(R/I)\cong V(I)\subseteq\Spec R,
\]
one has
\[
\boxed{
\Supp_{R/I}(M/IM)
=
\Supp_R(M)\cap V(I).
}
\]
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
Let \(\frakp\supseteq I\). Localizing gives
\[
(M/IM)_{\frakp}
\cong
M_{\frakp}/I_{\frakp}M_{\frakp}.
\]
If \(M_{\frakp}=0\), the quotient is zero. If \(M_{\frakp}\neq0\), then
\(I_{\frakp}\) lies in the maximal ideal of the local ring \(R_{\frakp}\). Nakayama's lemma shows that
\(M_{\frakp}/I_{\frakp}M_{\frakp}\neq0\). The stated equality follows.
records.proof_route: For a prime of R/I, pull it back to R. Construct the localization/quotient comparison and apply Nakayama to the localized finite module.
records.acceptance: At each q in Spec(R/I), nonvanishing of the quotient localization iff nonvanishing at its pulled-back prime. Then derive the image equality in Spec R.
records.formalization_questions: The two supports live in different spectra. State a preimage equality or an image equality through the quotient spectral map, never a raw equality between different types.
records.coverage_note: Actual M/(I • top) with its R/I action. Both the preimage equality and the exact image equality in Spec R are checked. Noetherianity is unnecessary.
records.review_verdict: proved as written

records.title: Ordinary patching datum

records.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Ordinary patching datum]\label{def:ordinary_patching_datum}
An ordinary patching datum consists of a Noetherian ring \(R_\infty\), an ideal
\(\fraka\subseteq R_\infty\), a finite \(R_\infty\) module \(M_\infty\), and identifications
\[
R\cong R_\infty/\fraka,
\qquad
M\cong M_\infty/\fraka M_\infty.
\]
In automorphy lifting applications, \(R_\infty\) is a patched deformation ring and \(M_\infty\) is a patched automorphic module. The definition itself contains no automorphy assertion.
\end{definition}

\]

records.title: Freeness over auxiliary variables is not enough
records.label: ex:freeness_not_support
records.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[Freeness over auxiliary variables is not enough]\label{ex:freeness_not_support}
Let \(k\) be a field, let \(S=k[[t]]\), and put
\[
R=S[[x]]/(x(x-t)).
\]
The ring \(R\) is reduced and has two irreducible components. Let
\[
M=R/(x)\cong S.
\]
Then \(M\) is free of rank one over \(S\), but
\[
\Supp_R(M)=V(x)
\]
is only one component of \(\Spec R\). Thus freeness over the auxiliary power series ring does not imply full support over the deformation ring.
\end{example}
records.proof_tex:
The two nonassociate prime factors \(x\) and \(x-t\) occur with multiplicity one, so the principal quotient is reduced. The displayed isomorphism makes \(M\) free over \(S\). Its annihilator as an \(R\) module is \((x)\), hence
\[
\Supp_R(M)=V(x)
\]
by \cref{thm:finite_module_support}. The generic point \((x-t)\) of the other component does not contain \(x\), so it is not in the support.

records.title: Derived support
records.label: def:derived_support
records.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Derived support]\label{def:derived_support}
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(C\) be a perfect complex of \(R\) modules. Its derived support is
\[
\Supp_R(C)
=
\left\{
\frakp\in\Spec R:
C\mathbin{\mathop{\otimes}\limits_R^{\mathbf L}}\kappa(\frakp)
\not\simeq0
\right\}.
\]
\end{definition}

records.title: Cohomological description of derived support
records.label: fact:derived_support_cohomology
records.statement_tex:
\begin{standardfact}[Cohomological description of derived support]\label{fact:derived_support_cohomology}
If \(R\) is Noetherian and \(C\) is perfect, then
\[
\Supp_R(C)
=
\bigcup_i\Supp_R H^i(C).
\]
In particular, derived support is closed and is empty exactly when \(C\simeq0\) \cite{Weibel1994,Eisenbud1995}.
\end{standardfact}

records.title: Derived quotient support
records.label: thm:derived_quotient_support
records.proof_tex:
Let \(\frakp\supseteq I\). Associativity of the derived tensor product gives
\[
\left(
C\mathbin{\mathop{\otimes}\limits_R^{\mathbf L}}R/I
\right)
\mathbin{\mathop{\otimes}\limits_{R/I}^{\mathbf L}}
\kappa(\frakp)
\simeq
C\mathbin{\mathop{\otimes}\limits_R^{\mathbf L}}\kappa(\frakp).
\]
The two fibers vanish simultaneously, which proves the equality.
records.proof_route: Represent a perfect complex by a bounded complex of finite projectives. Construct derived scalar base change and the residue-field fiber associator; prove invariance under the choice of model.
records.acceptance: The support pullback equality for the actual derived quotient. No Noetherian hypothesis is required by the printed theorem.
records.formalization_questions: Ordinary tensor of cohomology is not derived base change. An abstract associativity hypothesis can support an interface lemma only, until the actual derived associator is constructed.
records.coverage_note: A perfect complex is represented by an actual bounded complex of finitely generated projective modules. Its scalar extension is formed termwise and then mapped into Mathlib's actual derived category. Actual derived isomorphisms between projective models lift to homotopy equivalences, so arbitrary scalar extension and residue-field support are independent of the chosen model. The cochain tensor associator and faithful field extension give the support pullback; the actual quotient-spectrum contraction gives its ambient-spectrum image as Supp(C) intersect V(I). The result allows every commutative ring and ideal, with no Noetherian hypothesis. The original statement remains unchanged; the expanded proof is recorded separately.
records.review_verdict: proved as written in the declared context
records.revised_proof_tex:
Choose a bounded complex \(P\) of finite projective \(R\) modules representing \(C\). Scalar extension to a commutative \(R\) algebra \(S\) is computed degree by degree as \(S\otimes_RP\); the canonical symmetry of tensor products gives the displayed order \(C\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}S\). Scalar extension preserves the bounds, finite generation, and projectivity of the terms. A derived isomorphism between two such projective models lifts to a homotopy equivalence, which scalar extension preserves. The resulting derived object and its residue field fibers are therefore independent of the chosen model.

Let \(q\in\Spec(R/I)\), and let \(\frakp\) be its inverse image in \(R\). The composite point \(R\to R/I\to\kappa(q)\) has kernel \(\frakp\), so it factors through a field embedding \(\kappa(\frakp)\to\kappa(q)\). The ordinary tensor associator in every degree gives an isomorphism of complexes
\[
\kappa(q)\otimes_{R/I}\bigl((R/I)\otimes_RP\bigr)
\cong\kappa(q)\otimes_RP
\cong\kappa(q)\otimes_{\kappa(\frakp)}
\bigl(\kappa(\frakp)\otimes_RP\bigr).
\]
Extension of fields is faithfully flat. It preserves and reflects exactness in each degree, hence also acyclicity. The left hand complex is thus nonzero in the derived category exactly when the residue field fiber of \(C\) at \(\frakp\) is nonzero. This proves the support identity on corresponding primes. The image of \(\Spec(R/I)\to\Spec R\) is exactly \(V(I)\), giving the stated ambient spectrum equality, including the case \(I=R\).

records.title: Derived patching support descent
records.label: thm:derived_support_descent
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Derived patching support descent]\label{thm:derived_support_descent}
Let \((R_\infty,\fraka,C_\infty,R,C)\) be a derived patching datum. If
\[
\Supp_{R_\infty}(C_\infty)=\Spec R_\infty,
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
\Supp_R(C)=\Spec R.
}
\]
For every point \(x:R\to E'\) to a field, the derived fiber
\[
C\mathbin{\mathop{\otimes}\limits_{R,x}^{\mathbf L}}E'
\]
is nonzero.
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
The support equality follows from \cref{thm:derived_quotient_support}. The point
\(x\) has kernel \(\frakp\in\Spec R\). Since \(\frakp\) lies in the full support, the fiber over \(\kappa(\frakp)\) is nonzero. Extending scalars from \(\kappa(\frakp)\) to \(E'\) preserves nonvanishing for a bounded complex of finite dimensional vector spaces.

records.coverage_note: The derived patching datum records an actual quotient ring isomorphism and an actual derived-category isomorphism between the finite-level perfect complex and its patched scalar extension. Model invariance transports support through this comparison. Full support descends, and every field-valued point factors through the residue field at its kernel. Faithful scalar extension reflects acyclicity, proving nonvanishing of the actual specialized derived object. No fiber comparison or model invariance is supplied as an extra assumption. The original statement remains unchanged; the expanded proof is recorded separately.

records.revised_proof_tex:
Apply \cref{thm:derived_quotient_support} to the patched complex and use the actual ring identification \(R\cong R_\infty/\fraka\). Full patched support restricts to \(V(\fraka)\), which corresponds to all of \(\Spec R\). The supplied derived isomorphism with \(C\) preserves this support by the projective model argument in that theorem.

For a field valued point \(x:R\to E'\), put \(\frakp=\ker x\). The point factors as \(R\to\kappa(\frakp)\to E'\), where the second map is a field embedding. Tensor association on a projective model identifies the fiber at \(x\) with the extension to \(E'\) of the fiber at \(\frakp\). The latter is nonzero by full support. Faithful flatness of the field extension reflects exactness in every degree, so the fiber at \(x\) is nonzero as well. This applies to every field valued point, with no closed point restriction.

records.title: Support and Fitting transport
records.label: thm:rt_support_transport
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Support and Fitting transport]\label{thm:rt_support_transport}
Let \(\varphi:R\to\TT\) be an isomorphism of Noetherian rings. Let \(M\) be a finite \(\TT\) module, viewed as an \(R\) module through \(\varphi\). Then the homeomorphism
\[
\varphi^*:\Spec\TT\longrightarrow\Spec R
\]
satisfies
\[
\boxed{
\varphi^*\bigl(\Supp_{\TT}(M)\bigr)
=
\Supp_R(M).
}
\]
For every \(j\geq0\),
\[
\boxed{
\varphi
\left(
\Fitt_j^R(M)
\right)
=
\Fitt_j^{\TT}(M).
}
\]
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex: Localization commutes with transport along an isomorphism, so a localization of \(M\) vanishes on one side exactly when the corresponding localization vanishes on the other. This proves the support identity. A finite presentation matrix over \(R\) is carried entry by entry to a presentation matrix over \(\TT\). The minors generating each Fitting ideal are therefore carried to the corresponding minors.

records.title: Artin decomposition
records.label: fact:artin_decomposition
records.statement_tex:
\begin{standardfact}[Artin decomposition]\label{fact:artin_decomposition}
Let \(E'\) be a field and let \(\TT\) be a finite dimensional commutative
\(E'\) algebra. Then
\[
\boxed{
\TT
\cong
\prod_{\frakm\in\Max\TT}\TT_{\frakm}.
}
\]
Each factor is an Artin local algebra. Equivalently, there is a unique complete family of central idempotents \((e_{\frakm})\) such that
\[
e_{\frakm}e_{\mathfrak n}=0
\quad(\frakm\neq\mathfrak n),
\qquad
\sum_{\frakm}e_{\frakm}=1,
\]
and \(e_{\frakm}\TT\cong\TT_{\frakm}\) \cite{AtiyahMacdonald1969,Matsumura1989}.
\end{standardfact}

records.title: Simultaneous generalized eigenspaces
records.label: cor:simultaneous_generalized_eigenspaces
records.statement_tex:
\begin{corollary}[Simultaneous generalized eigenspaces]\label{cor:simultaneous_generalized_eigenspaces}
Assume that \(E'\) is algebraically closed and that \(\TT\) is generated by commuting operators \(T_1,\ldots,T_d\) on \(V\). For a maximal ideal
\[
\frakm
=
(T_1-\lambda_1,\ldots,T_d-\lambda_d),
\]
there is an integer \(N\geq1\) such that
\[
\boxed{
e_{\frakm}V
=
\left\{
v\in V:
(T_i-\lambda_i)^Nv=0
\text{ for every }i
\right\}.
}
\]
Thus the canonical Artin packet is the simultaneous generalized eigenspace.
\end{corollary}
records.proof_tex:
The maximal ideal of the Artin local algebra \(\TT_{\frakm}\) is nilpotent. Hence a common power of every \(T_i-\lambda_i\) kills the local packet. On every other local factor, at least one \(T_i-\lambda_i\) is a unit, so no nonzero vector can satisfy all the displayed nilpotence conditions.

records.title: A nonsemisimple Hecke packet
records.label: ex:nonsemisimple_hecke_packet
records.statement_tex:
\begin{example}[A nonsemisimple Hecke packet]\label{ex:nonsemisimple_hecke_packet}
Let
\[
\TT
=
E'[u]/(u^2)
\times
E'[v]/(v^3)
\]
and let \(V=\TT\) be the regular module. The two canonical central idempotents split
\[
V=V_u\oplus V_v
\]
with dimensions two and three. Multiplication by \(u\) is nilpotent on \(V_u\), and multiplication by \(v\) is nilpotent on \(V_v\). Neither local factor is semisimple, but the two maximal Hecke packets are isolated exactly by the Artin idempotents.
\end{example}
records.proof_tex: The product decomposition gives the two central idempotents \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\). Their ranges are the two local factors. The classes of \(u\) and \(v\) are nilpotent of orders two and three, respectively.

records.title: Nested packets in one finite carrier
records.label: thm:nested_finite_carrier
records.proof_tex:
The displayed relations give
\[
e_{m+1}V\subseteq e_mV.
\]
The nonnegative dimensions form a nonincreasing sequence of positive integers, so they eventually become constant. Once two consecutive dimensions agree, the corresponding inclusion is equality. Thus the ranges stabilize at a nonzero subspace, which is their intersection.
records.proof_route: Deduce antitonicity of ranges from the absorption laws. Prove eventual constancy of their natural-number dimensions, then use inclusion and equal finite rank to identify all sufficiently late ranges.
records.acceptance: There exists N such that every later range equals range(e_N), and the intersection is nonzero when all ranges are nonzero.
records.formalization_questions: One pair of equal consecutive dimensions does not by itself rule out a later drop. The proof must obtain eventual constancy of the whole sequence.

records.checked_proof_route: Finite-dimensional modules are Artinian; apply descending-chain stabilization, identify the stable term with the intersection, and use nonzero ranges.

\]
then \(e_mV=0\) for some finite \(m\).

records.title: Stable core
records.label: def:stable_core
records.statement_tex:
\begin{definition}[Stable core]\label{def:stable_core}
Let
\[
V_1\longleftarrow V_2\longleftarrow V_3\longleftarrow\cdots
\]
be an inverse system of finite dimensional vector spaces. For \(n\geq m\), write
\(f_{n,m}:V_n\to V_m\). The stable core at level \(m\) is
\[
Y_m
=
\bigcap_{n\geq m}\im(f_{n,m}).
\]
\end{definition}
records.coverage_note: Definition checked; excluded from the 49 internal theorem claims. The empty image-index family before the target contributes top.

records.title: Surjectivity on stable cores
records.label: lem:stable_core_surjectivity
records.proof_tex:
Fix \(y\in Y_m\). For \(n\geq m+1\), let
\[
A_n
=
\left\{
z\in\im(f_{n,m+1}):
f_{m+1,m}(z)=y
\right\}.
\]
Each \(A_n\) is a nonempty affine subspace of \(V_{m+1}\), and the sequence
\((A_n)\) is descending. A descending sequence of affine subspaces in a finite dimensional vector space stabilizes whenever every term is nonempty. Choose an element in its stable value. It lies in \(Y_{m+1}\) and maps to \(y\).
records.proof_route: Construct composites of the actual adjacent linear maps. For y in Y_m, use the nonempty descending affine fibers inside V_(m+1), whose dimensions stabilize, to find a preimage in every eventual image.
records.acceptance: A well-defined linear map Y_(m+1) -> Y_m and its surjectivity, without assuming ambient transition surjectivity.
records.formalization_questions: Finite dimensionality is required separately at each level; no uniform dimension bound is assumed.
records.coverage_note: The map is the restriction of the actual inverse-system transition to the actual intersection of later images. Surjectivity follows from eventual stabilization of the image chain at the next level. No ambient surjectivity or uniform dimension bound is assumed.
records.review_verdict: proved as written
records.checked_proof_route: Stabilize the transition images in V_(m+1), lift y from a sufficiently late level, then use the inverse-system composition law.

records.title: Nonzero stable core criterion
records.label: thm:nonzero_stable_core
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Nonzero stable core criterion]\label{thm:nonzero_stable_core}
Let \((V_m)\) be an inverse system of finite dimensional vector spaces. If
\[
Y_m\neq0
\]
for every \(m\), then
\[
\boxed{
\varprojlim_mV_m
\neq0.
}
\]
More precisely, the inverse limit contains a compatible sequence whose first coordinate is any prescribed nonzero element of \(Y_1\).
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
Choose \(0\neq y_1\in Y_1\). By \cref{lem:stable_core_surjectivity}, choose recursively
\(y_{m+1}\in Y_{m+1}\) mapping to \(y_m\). Every \(y_m\) is nonzero because it maps to the nonzero vector \(y_1\). The sequence \((y_m)\) is a nonzero element of the inverse limit.
records.proof_route: Recursively choose preimages within stable cores, beginning with the prescribed nonzero element. Prove compatibility and that every coordinate maps to that first element.
records.acceptance: An actual compatible vector family with the requested first coordinate, and nontriviality of the inverse-limit module.
records.formalization_questions: Nonempty would be vacuous for a vector-space limit because the zero branch exists. Preserve a nonzero coordinate witness.
records.coverage_note: The inverse limit is a submodule of the dependent product cut out by compatibility with every transition. A prescribed nonzero first stable-core vector extends to a sequence with every coordinate nonzero. Classical choice selects the recursively proved preimages. The first core alone being nonzero suffices.
records.review_verdict: proved as written
records.checked_proof_route: Recursively lift within the proved surjective stable-core maps; prove all-transition compatibility and preserve the prescribed nonzero first coordinate.

records.title: Surjective systems
records.label: cor:surjective_inverse_system
records.proof_tex: Surjectivity gives \(Y_m=V_m\). Apply \cref{thm:nonzero_stable_core}.
records.proof_route: Prove every composite transition surjective, hence every stable core equals the full level, and instantiate the preceding theorem.
records.acceptance: Nontrivial inverse limit for nontrivial finite-dimensional levels and surjective adjacent maps.
records.coverage_note: Adjacent surjectivity implies every composite is surjective and each stable core is the full space. In the finite-dimensional inverse-system context, nontriviality of the first space alone suffices for a nontrivial limit.
records.review_verdict: proved as written
records.checked_proof_route: Induct on composites to prove surjectivity, identify each core with the whole level, and apply the nonzero first-core theorem.

records.title: Chebotarev and Brauer Nesbitt identification
records.label: fact:chebotarev_brauer_nesbitt
records.statement_tex:
\begin{standardfact}[Chebotarev and Brauer Nesbitt identification]\label{fact:chebotarev_brauer_nesbitt}
Let \(E'\) be a characteristic zero field. Let
\[
\rho_1,\rho_2:G_{F,S}\longrightarrow\GL_n(E')
\]
be continuous semisimple representations. If their characteristic polynomials agree at every Frobenius element outside a density zero exceptional set, then
\[
\boxed{\rho_1\cong\rho_2.}
\]
This follows from Chebotarev density and the Brauer Nesbitt theorem
\cite{BrauerNesbitt1941,Neukirch1999}.
\end{standardfact}

records.title: Support gives a Hecke eigensystem
records.label: thm:support_gives_hecke_system
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Support gives a Hecke eigensystem]\label{thm:support_gives_hecke_system}
Let \(R\cong\TT\), let \(H\) be a finite \(\TT\) module, and let
\(x:R\to E'\) be a field valued point. If
\[
\ker x\in\Supp_R(H),
\]
then
\[
\boxed{
H_x:=H\otimes_{\TT,x}E'\neq0.
}
\]
Every element of \(\TT\) acts on \(H_x\) through the scalar prescribed by \(x\).
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex:
Nonvanishing follows from \cref{cor:supported_hecke_fiber}. The tensor product relation
\[
th\otimes1=h\otimes x(t)
\]
shows that \(t\in\TT\) acts through \(x(t)\).
records.proof_route: Use nontriviality of the actual field fiber and the tensor balancing relation to show each Hecke element acts by its point value.
records.acceptance: Nonzero fiber and the scalar-action identity on every tensor, not only on pure tensors.
records.formalization_questions: For phi:R equiv T and x:R->E, the Hecke scalar is (x composed with phi inverse)(t).
records.coverage_note: Nonzero actual Hecke tensor fiber plus equality of actual induced Hecke endomorphisms with the prescribed scalar operators. The operator is defined by base change of h ↦ t • h, not by declaring it to be the desired scalar action.

records.title: Pointwise Galois realization
records.label: thm:pointwise_galois_realization
records.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Pointwise Galois realization]\label{thm:pointwise_galois_realization}
Assume the following data.
\begin{enumerate}
\item A represented deformation ring \(R\) with universal representation
\[
\rho_R:G_{F,S}\longrightarrow\GL_n(R).
\]
\item An isomorphism \(R\cong\TT\).
\item An automorphic Hecke datum \((\TT,H,(P_v))\).
\item A characteristic zero point \(x:R\to E'\) lying in \(\Supp_R(H)\).
\item A classical automorphic representation \(\pi_x\) occurring in the fiber \(H_x\), together with a semisimple attached representation
\[
\rho_{\pi_x}:G_{F,S}\longrightarrow\GL_n(E')
\]
whose unramified characteristic polynomial is \(x(P_v(X))\).
\item Equality
\[
\det\left(X-\rho_x(\Frob_v)\right)=x(P_v(X))
\]
for \(\rho_x=x\circ\rho_R\) at every unramified place in a Chebotarev dense set.
\end{enumerate}
Then
\[
\boxed{
\rho_x^{\mathrm{ss}}
\cong
\rho_{\pi_x}.
}
\]
If \(\rho_x\) is irreducible, then \(\rho_x\cong\rho_{\pi_x}\).
\end{theorem}
records.proof_tex: The two semisimple representations have the same characteristic polynomials on a Chebotarev dense set. Apply \cref{fact:chebotarev_brauer_nesbitt}. If \(\rho_x\) is irreducible, it is already semisimple.
records.proof_route: Retain the supplied classical automorphic object, its attached semisimple representation, and matching Frobenius polynomials. Apply a typed, explicitly external Chebotarev/Brauer–Nesbitt identification input. Handle the irreducible case separately.
records.acceptance: An isomorphism between rho_x semisimplified and the attached representation, with the exact coefficient field and Frobenius set.
records.formalization_questions: This is conditional. Do not replace the external input by a custom global axiom or assume the final isomorphism itself. Specify coefficient topology and the precise dense-set identification contract before claiming arithmetic coverage.
records.coverage_note: The actual universal matrix representation is specialized along the field-valued point. Continuity of its actual characteristic-polynomial coefficients and conjugacy invariance extend matching Frobenius data to the whole group. The universal algebraic Brauer–Nesbitt input then supplies an actual invertible linear intertwiner to the attached semisimple representation. Semisimplification choice-independence and the irreducible conclusion are derived. Original wording lacks explicit Hausdorff coefficient topology and specialization continuity; those hypotheses are now an explicit amendment.

\right)

amendment.statement_tex:
\begin{theorem}[Conditional simultaneous companion completion]\label{thm:simultaneous_companion_completion}
Under the coefficient and finite admissibility hypotheses above, one can choose continuous representations
\[
\rho_\lambda:\Gamma\longrightarrow\GL_D(\OO_\lambda)
\qquad(\lambda\in\Lambda)
\]
whose reduction class belongs to \(X_{\lambda,n}\) for every positive \(n\). They retain the declared residual class. After applying \(i_\lambda\), they are continuous, trivial on \(H_\lambda\), and satisfy
\[
\det\!\left(X- i_\lambda(\rho_\lambda(\gamma_v))\right)
=e_\lambda(P_v),\qquad v\in\Omega_\lambda.
\]
Their integral evaluation points factor through every actual quotient \(B_\lambda/J_{\lambda,u}\).
\end{theorem}
amendment.proof_tex:
The finitely generated ideal and finite residue ring give finite coefficient quotients at every precision. An individual conjugacy class has finitely many frames because the group of invertible basis matrices over each quotient is finite. Thus the finitely many admissible classes give a finite nonempty set of actual continuous representations at each positive level. Continuity is invariant under conjugation. Reduction gives total maps between these sets. Compactness, as in \cref{thm:companion_branch_criterion}, selects strictly compatible representatives. This step neither assumes transition surjectivity nor lifts a prescribed conjugating matrix.

Completeness and separatedness identify \(\GL_D(\OO_\lambda)\) with the compatible inverse limit of the quotient matrix groups. Lift entries and inverse entries to construct this identification. The two reduction and reconstruction identities hold entrywise. Finite quotient continuity implies continuity for the ideal adic topology, including the matrix inverse, so the reconstructed representation is continuous.

Each coefficient of its characteristic polynomial agrees with the prescribed integral coefficient modulo every positive power of \(I_\lambda\). Separatedness gives equality of the full polynomials. The same argument applied to the matrix entries of \(\rho_\lambda(g)-1\) gives triviality on \(H_\lambda\). Continuous coefficient change and the matching equations for \(P_{\lambda,v}\) give the asserted common spine over the local fields.

For \(p\in J_{\lambda,u}\), evaluation commutes with reduction. Its value is zero modulo every positive power of \(I_\lambda\), hence is zero integrally by separatedness. Therefore the evaluation homomorphism kills the whole ideal and factors uniquely through \(B_\lambda/J_{\lambda,u}\). Choose a realization for each \(\lambda\).

Finite forests alone give compatible classes. To obtain actual continuous representations, we use the following explicit coefficient and admissibility data. They also delimit the meaning of completion in the next theorem.

Fix a topological group \(\Gamma\), a finite matrix index set \(D\), and a set \(\Lambda\) of coefficient indices. For each \(\lambda\), let \(\OO_\lambda\) be a commutative ring, complete and separated for a finitely generated ideal \(I_\lambda\), with finite residue ring \(\OO_\lambda/I_\lambda\). Give \(\OO_\lambda\) its ideal adic topology and every quotient its discrete topology. Let
\[
i_\lambda:\OO_\lambda\longrightarrow K_\lambda,
\qquad e_\lambda:L\longrightarrow K_\lambda
\]
be supplied ring homomorphisms, where \(L\) and \(K_\lambda\) are fields, \(K_\lambda\) has a declared topology, and \(i_\lambda\) is continuous.

For every positive integer \(n\), let \(X_{\lambda,n}\) be a finite nonempty set of conjugacy classes of actual continuous representations
\[

\]
Conjugacy means change of basis by an invertible matrix over that quotient. Assume reduction preserves these sets and that \(X_{\lambda,1}\) consists of the declared residual class. \]

Also supply a subgroup \(H_\lambda\leq\Gamma\) on which all these finite representations are trivial. This is an inertia condition when \(H_\lambda\) is the specified inertia subgroup.

\[
B_\lambda=\OO_\lambda[x_{g,a,b}:g\in\Gamma,\ a,b\in D].

records.title: Failure of integral sign projectors

records.statement_tex:
\begin{proposition}[Failure of integral sign projectors]\label{prop:dyadic_sign_projectors}
Let \(C_2=\langle g\rangle\). Over \(\QQ_2\), the two sign projectors are
\[
\boxed{
e_+=\frac{1+g}{2},
\qquad
e_-=\frac{1-g}{2}.
}
\]
Neither belongs to \(\ZZ_2[C_2]\). After reduction modulo two,
\[
\boxed{
\FF_2[C_2]
\cong
\FF_2[X]/(X^2),
\qquad
X=g-1.
}
\]
This ring is local and has no nontrivial idempotents.
\end{proposition}
records.proof_tex:
The displayed rational elements are the unique primitive idempotents because they project to the two characters of \(C_2\). Their coefficients contain \(1/2\), so they are not integral. In characteristic two,
\[
(g-1)^2=g^2-2g+1=0.
\]
The map \(X\mapsto g-1\) gives the displayed isomorphism. The quotient by \((X)\) is \(\FF_2\), and \((X)\) is nilpotent. Thus the ring is local.
